claims.text: A machine-learning model driven by binary-phase-diagram-inspired parameters can be applied to predict electrical conductivity in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The model explicitly incorporates the effects of oxygen-induced defects.
The model will predict temperature-dependent electrical conductivity more accurately than analytical perfect-crystal models in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The proposed samples are nominally pure bulk HfNbTaTiZr and bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Phase-diagram-derived parameters can account for intrinsic compositional variations affecting electronic transport.
Phase-diagram-derived parameters can account for extrinsic oxygen-defect effects on electronic transport.
Testing should cover 0–200 K and 300–1200 K under vacuum or a controlled atmosphere.
Oxygen impurities create defect complexes in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced defect complexes modify the local electronic structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced defect complexes modify the phase stability of HfNbTaTiZr.
Binary-phase-diagram-inspired parameters capture the conductivity-relevant effects of oxygen-induced defect structures.
Analytical conductivity models based on perfect, defect-free crystals overlook real-sample oxygen-defect effects.
The machine-learning predictions will be within approximately 10% of measured conductivity.
Traditional analytical predictions may deviate from measured conductivity by more than 20%.
The proposed approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Applicability above 1 wt.% oxygen, outside the specified temperature ranges, or to other alloy systems is uncertain.
The exact reduction in prediction error and the detailed oxygen-defect transport mechanism remain uncertain.

The hypothesis is falsified if the machine-learning model fails to produce a statistically significant error reduction relative to the analytical model or fails to remain within roughly 10% of measurements.
